Iran says ready to reopen Hormuz in two days if US agrees to demands
item.description:
Iran on Monday said it was ready to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if Washington agrees to conditions, as US President Donald Trump issued his latest war threat at a rally for midterm elections.
A senior Iranian official said the offer to open the vital energy corridor, which follows intense efforts by mediators to stop a return to war, showed “good faith.”
Tehran has blockaded Hormuz since the war started in February, sending energy prices soaring and posing an electoral challenge for Trump. The narrow gateway to the energy-rich Gulf normally carries one-fifth of global oil consumption.
“The possibility of implementing this plan in two days is another indication of Iran’s good-faith approach,” foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei told reporters at a briefing.
“We have stated that, if Iran’s demands are met, it would be possible to restore security to the Strait of Hormuz and resume the negotiating process within a short period.”
In September, Iran proposed a seven-day plan to reopen Hormuz if the US agreed to demands including ending the war on all fronts, unfreezing Iranian assets, lifting oil sanctions and ending its counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
Baqaei said messages were being exchanged with the United States via mediators, adding that “everything depends” on the US side accepting the Iranian demands.
“Only then can we discuss the subsequent stages.”
During final rallies for the US midterms on Tuesday, where diesel prices and consumer inflation are a key issue, Trump struck a belligerent tone, warning Iran to expect “the hammer.”
“The only reason why I’m not finished with Iran is I want to be nice. I want to try and save all those lives if I can... But at some point we’re going to have to give them the hammer,” he told voters in Iowa.
Officials from Pakistan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye have held talks with Iran in recent days, while US Vice President JD Vance sent a letter to Tehran.
Oman’s ruler Sultan Haitham bin Tariq discussed the war with Chinese President Xi Jinping during a visit to Beijing on Monday, an Omani foreign ministry statement said.
“The two sides called for resolving disputes through political and diplomatic means, urging the United States and Iran to pursue a peaceful path, achieve a ceasefire (and) prevent war entirely,” it said, calling for “dialogue and negotiations as soon as possible,”
China’s top diplomat also told a senior Iranian official that Beijing supports Tehran in “safeguarding its own sovereignty and security,”
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi made the remarks to Ali Bagheri Kani, deputy secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, according to a statement from Beijing.
“All parties should... in a spirit of reason and pragmatism, focus on a political solution rather than once again resorting to armed conflict,” Wang was cited as saying.
Bagheri told Wang that “Tehran’s stance on defending its national security, sovereignty, and territorial integrity remains unchanged, and that Iran will make no compromises in this regard,” according to state TV.
In an interview with Al Jazeera released on Sunday, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Washington must accept a new route agreed between Iran and Oman for transiting the strait.
He said the US must also remove sanctions imposed in recent months and reduce American troop numbers in the region.
Washington has since August rolled out a fresh raft of sanctions, part of what it called “economic asphyxiation” of Iran.
Trump’s “hammer” comment is just the latest threat to Tehran from the US and Israel, whose joint attack marked the start of the war on February 28.
On Saturday, Trump said he still had to “take care” of one or two targets including Pickaxe mountain in central Iran, a suspected nuclear site which Tehran denies is such a facility.
“Any act of aggression against Iran, any military attack against Iran, by whatever means, will be met with a powerful, immediate and comprehensive response from us,” Baqaei said.
At the midterms, Democrats expect to win at least partial control of Congress and impose political constraints on Trump for the first time in two years.

item.title: Ukraine, Russia see emergency alert systems hacked
item.description:
Emergency alert systems in Russia and Ukraine were hit in cyberattacks overnight, with fake warnings of possible nuclear strikes broadcast to users in both countries.
The systems have since been brought back under control, though much remains unclear about the attacks, including who was responsible.
Phone notifications were sent to millions across Ukraine late Sunday warning of a “nuclear alert,” a “chemical threat” and even “street fights” in Kyiv.
One of the messages was in Russian and included a link to a new Telegram account named “Hitcore,” the logo of which is a metallic eagle emblazoned over the Russian tricolor flag.
Ukraine’s air force said the “air alert” app -- which typically warns of incoming Russian drone and missile attacks -- had been “subjected to hostile interference.”
Air force spokesman Yuri Ignat confirmed the hack to AFP.
A few hours later, Russia’s emergency situations ministry said that a “massive cyberattack” had hit its own application, with “false information” sent to the public.
Several regional social media accounts run by the department sent out messages warning of a imminent nuclear attack on Russia.
For instance, a Telegram message was sent by authorities in the Belgorod border region warning “nuclear warheads ... have been launched at all regions of Russia,” and telling people to “urgently stock up on food for three weeks.”
Ukraine’s air alert app is widely used to warn of Russian missile and drone attacks. It has been downloaded more than 46 million times and has more than 6.7 million daily users, according to developers, Ajax Systems.
Made with support from the digital transformation ministry, it uses air force data to send mobile notifications at the same time country-wide sirens and loudspeakers announce the start of an air raid, urging people to seek shelter.
The alerts blare out day and night in almost all regions of the country.
The hack did not affect other alert systems or government-backed apps that deliver drone and missile warnings.
The app developers temporarily disabled notifications before saying Monday that operations had been restored.
Russia does not have a nationwide air alert system, and beyond border regions does not routinely send warnings to citizens of incoming Ukrainian attacks.
Few Russians use the affected application, run by the ministry of emergency situations.
Some regional authorities, which take information from the ministry, appear to have either automatically posted the spoof message, or circulated the information on their social media channels.
It remains unclear if the attacks were part of the war, carried out by either side, or launched by independent actors or groups.
Ukraine’s Centre for Strategic Communication, a government-backed project set up to counter Russian propaganda and online threats, said “Russians have hacked” the app.
Air force spokesman Ignat told Ukrainian TV: “The Russians did indeed attack this app.”
A pro-Russian group calling itself Hitcore claimed responsibility for the hack of the Ukrainian alert system.
The group launched a Telegram channel shortly before the attack and included a link to the page in the first message it sent through the system.
One post on the page, addressed to Ukraine’s SBU security services and written in Russian said: “Your government is losing” and urged Kyiv’s spies to defect.
Nobody has claimed responsibility for the hack of the Russian system.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Monday that the threat of cyberattacks was growing due to the rise of artificial intelligence, adding that Moscow was taking “appropriate measures.”
He did not say who Russia believed was behind the incident.

item.title: Limited French school protests resume as holidays end
item.description:
French students returning from autumn holidays blocked some high schools on Monday, determined to reinvigorate a protest movement despite government concessions during the break.
Just one percent of France’s 3,700 high schools for 15 to 18-year-olds called lycées were blockaded, the education ministry said.
Pupils maintained their protest after hundreds of thousands of people, including students, took to the streets across France on Saturday for a third consecutive weekend of demonstrations.
The cost-of-living rallies emerged after high school students launched nationwide demonstrations in September over learning conditions and inequality.
The government has announced measures, including changing the university admissions process, ensuring more teachers and capping the number of pupils per class.
But some students say it is not enough.
In the southern city of Marseille, several garbage bins were stacked in front of the entrance to one high school on Monday morning.
“We’ve resumed the movement because we were supposedly given answers, but... it’s clearly not enough,” 16-year-old Meriem told AFP, perched on one of the dumpsters.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray told the France Inter radio station students should return to the classroom to avoid failing exams.
“I have students who are sitting the baccalaureate at the end of the year, and several hundred thousand of them haven’t attended classes for four or five weeks,” he said.
President Emmanuel Macron has called for classes to resume in a calm manner, arguing that “young people have been heard.”
With the European Union’s second-largest economy on the brink of recession and under pressure to rein in debt, the government has limited scope to appease student protesters through additional spending.

item.title: Iran warns new war could last longer after Trump threatens strikes
item.description:
Iran warned on Sunday that any renewed war with the United States could last longer than the previous round of fighting, after President Donald Trump said he still had to “take care” of more targets.
Diplomatic efforts to end the Middle East war have been punctuated by repeated threats from the United States and Israel to resume bombardments as they hold crucial elections.
“A potential future war could last longer than previous conflict, and the American president would not be in a position to dictate the timing or the conditions of its conclusion,” said army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia, according to Iranian state television.
In the most intense phase of the war, which began on February 28 with US-Israeli strikes on Iran, Tehran retaliated with missile and drone attacks across the region. Iran-aligned armed groups joined the fighting in Lebanon and Yemen.
Akraminia’s remarks followed Trump’s suggestion that the United States could swiftly strike its remaining targets in Iran.
“We still have to take care of, I would say one or two sites, but we can do that in 10 minutes,” Trump told reporters.
“You probably could look at Pickaxe Mountain, and you have to take care of that. We can do that all very quickly,” he added, referring to a suspected underground nuclear complex.
Trump reiterated his threat on Sunday, telling a campaign rally in Iowa ahead of midterm elections, that he may have to give Tehran “the hammer” at some unspecified time.
The warning came after US media reported that Trump had held a call with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday over whether and when to ramp up combat operations against the Islamic Republic.
Axios quoted one US and one Israeli official saying the two leaders discussed the state of negotiations with Iran, with Netanyahu pressing the president to strike the country immediately after Tuesday’s US midterm elections and Trump eager to let negotiations play out.
The Israeli source described the call as “tough,” while the US source said it was “direct,” according to Axios.
Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Trump confirmed he had discussed Iran with Netanyahu, but would not elaborate.
Top military and political officials in Iran have warned against any new attack.
Revolutionary Guards spokesman Hossein Mohebbi on Sunday echoed a warning issued a day earlier in a written message by Iran’s new supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei.
“In a conflict with America, there are no geographical limitations; a vast theatre has been defined for inflicting damage upon the enemy,” Mohebbi said, according to state television.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said: “We hope the other side will exercise rationality and choose diplomacy,” adding that Iran “remains prepared for both defense and diplomacy,” according to the official IRNA news agency.
The warnings came as Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei disclosed on Saturday that he had received a letter from US Vice President JD Vance seeking to revive talks.
Rezaei noted what he described as a positive change in “tone” from the US side but said he had yet to respond.
He said Tehran had previously told Washington that unless its conditions were met, “neither would the Strait of Hormuz be reopened nor would there be any negotiations.”
Those conditions include unfreezing Iranian assets abroad, ending the months-long US naval blockade of Iranian ports, lifting longstanding sanctions and ending the war on all fronts.
Since the war began, Iran has claimed control over the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global energy conduit, and repeatedly targeted vessels attempting to cross without its authorization.
The United States has imposed a naval counter-blockade on Iranian ports.
Anwar Gargash, diplomatic adviser to the Emirati president, said on Sunday that the United Arab Emirates hoped the exchanges would yield a breakthrough, but was preparing for the worst.
“It is not the interest of the region to go through another round... But I think we’re also, as we’ve shown before, braced for the worst,” he told a conference in Manama.
In Tehran, some residents described a sense of helplessness as threats of renewed fighting mount.
“The news coming in is truly worrying. However... there is nothing I can actually do about it,” Mohadese, a 27-year-old health inspector, told AFP.
Others including 48-year-old vendor Ebrahim saw no reason to be concerned.
“We do not fear another war; we have been at war for 48 years now -- we are always at war,” he said in downtown Tehran.

item.title: Taliban government voices ‘serious concern’ over US Afghan deportation plans
item.description:
Afghanistan’s Taliban authorities voiced concern on Monday over reported plans by Washington to deport scores of Afghan immigrants to Pakistan with the aim of their eventual return to their home country.
More than 150 Afghans in the United States would be deported via Pakistan to Afghanistan, including relatives of those who assisted US forces before their 2021 withdrawal, according to US media reports and an advocacy group.
“The Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan expresses its serious concern over reports that the United States intends to deport some Afghan refugees to Pakistan who have not yet been able to obtain legal residency documents in that country,” foreign ministry spokesman Abdul Qahar Balkhi said in a statement.
Advocacy groups have warned that the removal of former allies and their families could endanger their lives.
After regaining power, Taliban authorities announced a general amnesty for Afghans who worked with Western-backed forces and governments and have repeated promises this year that their former foes could safely return home.
However, the United Nations has recorded reports of extrajudicial killings, detentions and abuses.
President Donald Trump’s administration last year issued travel bans for a number of countries, including Afghanistan, as part of a broad immigration crackdown.
His administration sought to end deportation protections for Afghans, some of whom were granted special immigrant visas following the 2021 takeover by Taliban authorities.
Among those expected to be deported are relatives of Afghans who assisted the US military in the country prior to the fall of Kabul, according to AfghanEvac, a group seeking to help former Afghan allies.
While the United States cannot arrange deportations directly to Afghanistan, anonymous US officials told The New York Times that Pakistan will oversee their expulsion to Afghanistan.
In recent years, Germany and Turkey have deported Afghan nationals directly to Afghanistan, despite concerns from human rights groups over the risks facing returnees.
Balkhi said Taliban authorities urged “the United States of America to adopt a responsible and measured approach in this regard and to take any decisions and measures regarding the fate of Afghan citizens with clear mutual understanding, necessary coordination, and consideration of the rights and legitimate demands of the individuals concerned.”
“The Afghan side is ready to interact in this regard in a practical and mutually understanding manner,” he added.
Pakistan’s government earlier this year ordered law enforcement nationwide to arrest Afghan citizens without visas as part of a years-long repatriation policy that has pushed back millions of Afghans who fled throughout decades of war.
Relations between Pakistan and Afghanistan have been fraught since the Taliban authorities took power and worsened after deadly border clashes last October that led to near-total closure of the border.

item.title: Democrats, Trump hold final rallies before midterm elections
item.description:
Democrats teed up final get-out-the-vote rallies Monday on the eve of midterm elections where they expect to win at least partial control of Congress and impose political constraints on President Donald Trump for the first time in two years.
Rallies -- including by star Democratic Senate candidates James Talarico in Texas and Adam Hamilton in Kansas -- were capping a campaign of breathtaking tension and bitterness.
For his closing argument, Trump chose a speech in Washington at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool -- a landmark that has become synonymous with the 80-year-old president’s obsessive, controversial drive to redevelop the US capital.
“We’re going to win,” he said on Sunday.
Polls, however, show that Democrats are near certain to take the majority from Republicans in the House of Representatives and have a real shot at winning the currently Republican Senate.
Even winning just the House would mean Democrats have voting power over the federal budget and would lead powerful committees able to investigate alleged corruption under Trump, the Epstein files and other explosive issues.
The loss of total Republican dominance would push Trump into unfamiliar and uncomfortable territory: a lame-duck period beset with high inflation at home, the sputtering war against Iran and hostile Democratic investigations into his activities in Washington.
But a decade into the Trump era, Democrats remain wary about predictions of victory.
“Nauseously optimistic,” Democratic Senator Raphael Warnock told CNN to describe the mood.
Democrats are facing late internal divisions, with left-wing candidates clashing at times with the party’s establishment.
In a startling display of infighting on Sunday, Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens in Michigan endorsed Republican candidate Mike Rogers against left-wing progressive candidate Abdul El-Sayed in her state’s key Senate race.
Trump was quick to praise Stevens for her “bravery,” posting on his Truth Social platform that “Haley said what few people are willing to say.”
Stevens, who lost a bruising primary to El-Sayed in August despite being backed by the Democratic establishment, struggled to explain her decision in an interview with CNN.
“It’s just where I was at the end of the night and earlier this morning,” she said.
Trump’s Republicans have fought a political scorched-earth campaign, painting Democrats as communists and openly branding El-Sayed, who is Muslim, as a terrorist.
Addressing a crowd in Iowa on Sunday, Trump said Democrats are “extreme and dangerous radicals” who will “steal your wealth” and let in migrants to “ransack, rape and plunder.”
But polls show Americans heavily souring on Trump’s wrecking-ball act.
An NBC News poll released on Sunday showed 60 percent disapprove of his performance, particularly over high prices exacerbated by his now eight-month-long war against Iran.
While the House seems highly likely to turn Democratic, the battle for the Senate is up in the air.
Only a third of the Senate’s 100 seats are being contested in these midterms, and few of the races were seen as favorable to Democrats.
However, with surprisingly strong challenges in deeply Republican states, pollsters now say the odds of a Democratic flip are at minimum even.
The final New York Times/Siena poll released Sunday evening showed Democratic candidates leading in all seven seats viewed as most competitive, though five remained within the margin of error.
A Democratic Senate would be able to shut down Trump’s lifetime appointments to courts -- including the Supreme Court.
While Tuesday is election day, early voting has already seen a record 54 million people cast ballots around the country.
The midterms have seen about $11 billion spent on advertising, with large chunks coming from individual mega-donors.
Elon Musk, a close Trump ally who led the so-called DOGE effort in dismantling entire government departments, has given a staggering nearly half-billion dollars to help get Republicans elected.

item.title: Mirpur police vehicle arson: Rashed Khan demands Jamaat chief’s arrest
item.description:
Prime Minister’s Political Assistant Rashed Khan on Monday demanded the arrest of Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami Ameer Dr Shafiqur Rahman, accusing him of instigating the arson attack on a police vehicle in Mirpur amid the garment workers’ demonstrations over wages.
“A police vehicle was set on fire in Mirpur. The Jamaat ameer should be arrested and brought to justice for this act of arson. As an instigator, he cannot evade responsibility for the incident,” Rashed said.
He made the demand while talking to reporters after a programme at the Jatiya Press Club.
Rashed alleged that Shafiqur had recently said if the people stood with Jamaat, the party would implement its seven-point demand and “smash everything of the government”.
“Awami League is hatching conspiracies, and Jamaat is behind these conspiracies. The party is instigating them. So, I believe the Jamaat ameer should be arrested over this arson attack and legal action should be taken against him,” the PM’s political assistant said.
Referring to the Jamaat ameer’s remarks at a recent long march and a subsequent Facebook post, he questioned the call for the government to take a tough stance.
“You said at the long march that everything would be smashed. Now you have posted on Facebook that the government must be tough. When you made that remark at the long march, did you not think about this?” Rashed asked.
He further alleged that the Jamaat chief could not evade responsibility for the alleged acts of anarchy, arson and violence being carried out by the “Awami League” across the country.
Meanwhile, garment workers continued demonstrations and blocked highways and major roads in Gazipur, Savar and Narayanganj on Monday, demanding a minimum monthly wage of Tk30,000.
At least two vehicles, including a police vehicle, were set on fire in Gazipur and Savar, while a Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) member and an Industrial Police officer were injured in clashes with workers.
The unrest continued despite the government's formation of a six-member minimum wage board on Sunday to review the wage structure for garment workers amid widespread protests in the country's industrial belts.

Milon: Education has no gender
item.description:
Education Minister Dr ANM Ehsanul Hoque Milon on Monday said education has no gender, questioning whether anyone in the world has ever said that people of a particular gender cannot receive education.
“Does education have any gender? Has anyone ever said that people of a particular gender can study while others cannot? I believe education has no gender,” he said.
The minister made the remarks while speaking as the chief guest at the certificate distribution and closing ceremony of the 210th Basic Training Course at the National Academy for Educational Management (NAEM) in Dhanmondi.
Referring to criticism over his earlier remarks on gender, Milon said a particular online newspaper had accused him of believing in transgender identity.
He said he had been discussing the representation of different gender identities in education and had cited data showing that the proportion of transgender people among those who qualified was less than one percent in that event.
The minister criticised what he described as the tendency of some media outlets to distort speakers' remarks and divert their intended meaning without listening to the full context.
“People should listen and understand before making comments. Creating panic in this way is very detrimental,” he said, urging the media to highlight positive developments alongside negative issues.
Speaking about the results of the SSC and HSC examinations, Milon said the country's education system had suffered a setback since the Covid-19 pandemic.
He said the practice of passing students without proper assessment had gradually weakened academic standards. He also referred to the impact of political developments and what he described as a growing tendency among students to become involved in politics instead of concentrating on their studies.
The minister said the BNP government is working to improve students' learning and writing skills, adding that weaknesses in higher education also needed attention.
Milon stressed the need for proper training and orientation for teachers, saying that unlike other cadres of the Bangladesh Civil Service, education cadre officers generally join their jobs without undergoing a structured training programme beforehand.
He said administrative cadre officers receive training after joining the service, while members of the armed forces and police also undergo professional training before taking up their responsibilities.
“Training makes people better. But teachers do not have that kind of training arrangement,” he said.
The minister said the government wanted to introduce a merit-based approach in training programmes, giving priority to those who perform well in presentations, classroom activities and assessments.
He said the basic training course needed to be made more comprehensive, as teaching models, modules and pedagogical approaches were gradually changing.
He said the government is considering how to make the best use of resources allocated to education.
The minister said Prime Minister Tarique Rahman had allocated the highest amount to the education sector, while the ministry was also working to ensure that the available resources were used effectively.
“We are working to build a future Bangladesh. The Prime Minister is working relentlessly towards that goal, and I have been given responsibility for this ministry to contribute to that effort,” he said.
He called upon everyone involved in education to think critically and analyse how the country's education system could be developed. “The collective thinking of all of us will be the driving force behind building the future Bangladesh,” he added.
Professor Prem Rizvi, Director (Training and Implementation) of NAEM, course adviser and convener of its Central Evaluation Committee, was also present at the event.
The programme was chaired by NAEM Director General Professor Dr Wasim Md Mezbahul Haque.

item.title: Salahuddin urges universities to lead in building technology-driven, merit-based society
item.description:
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed on Monday called upon the country's universities to play a leading role in building a technology-driven, merit- and knowledge-based society to meet the challenges of the 21st century and achieve the vision of a modern Bangladesh.
The minister stressed the need to go beyond conventional education and focus on technological knowledge, innovation and intellectual development.
He made the call while addressing a discussion meeting as the chief guest at the central auditorium of Jagannath University (JnU) in Dhaka today, marking the university's 21st founding anniversary.
He urged universities across the country to promote innovative research, modern information technology practices and merit-based education.
Emphasizing continuity in public welfare initiatives, Salahuddin said that development-oriented activities should continue despite political changes in the country.
"Bangladesh first, people first" should be the guiding principle, he said, adding that a country is not merely defined by its territory or flag but also by the people's rights, ownership and participation.
Recalling the history of Jagannath University, the minister said that efforts to transform the institution into a university began in 1995 through the initiatives of Shaheed student leader Nasiruddin Pintu and others, alongside the commitment of former Prime Minister Begum Khaleda Zia.
Subsequently, in 2005, during the BNP government's tenure, an act was passed in Parliament to upgrade Jagannath University College into a full-fledged university.
He also mentioned that construction of a separate modern campus with residential facilities on 200 acres of land in Keraniganj is underway.
He assured students that the government maintains a positive attitude towards addressing their reasonable demands.
On higher education, the minister said that academic certificates and GPA-5 results alone cannot ensure national development.
Qualitative improvements in education and a stronger focus on research are essential, he stated.
He noted that universities should not function merely as institutions for preparing graduates for employment but should also serve as centers of intellectual freedom, advanced research, and knowledge creation.
Highlighting the importance of technical and vocational education, he urged students to develop practical skills and professional expertise in line with the demands of the modern world rather than pursuing conventional academic degrees without adequate employment opportunities.
Referring to the growing importance of the semiconductor industry, artificial intelligence (AI), and technology-driven economies, the minister said that innovative ideas, technological knowledge and a skilled workforce are indispensable for Bangladesh to remain competitive in the future.

item.title: 14 teachers, one student – and the only examinee fails
item.description:
A college in Muksudpur upazila of Gopalganj, with 14 teachers but only one HSC examinee this year, has recorded a zero pass rate after its sole candidate failed the examination.
Durbashur Adarsha Secondary School and College was among the institutions under the Dhaka Education Board where no students passed the Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) examination, results of which were published on Saturday.
According to college sources, only one student enrolled in the 2025-26 academic session and appeared in this year's HSC examination. The student failed, leaving the institution with a zero pass rate.
The result has sparked criticism among local residents, who blamed the institution's management committee, principal and teachers for its poor academic performance.
Local residents Balaram Ojha, Nirmal Biswas and Shubhendu Sarkar said students were reluctant to enroll because the institution lacked a proper learning environment.
They questioned how the college could continue operating in such a condition and suggested that its college section be shut down.
Established in 1988, the institution initially operated as a secondary school. Its college section was introduced in 2009, offering science, humanities and business studies.
All 14 teachers are enrolled under the government's Monthly Pay Order (MPO) scheme and receive regular salaries and allowances. The same teachers have also been conducting classes for the college section.
However, only the humanities group had an examinee this year, while the science and business studies groups had no enrolled students.
Principal Swarna Rani Biswas said the institution struggled to attract students because of its rural location.
"Students are hard to find as the college is in a village. Teachers also do not come regularly or show much interest in enrolling students. I have been trying to improve the situation and spending money from my own pocket every year, but nothing has worked," she said.
Founder Paritosh Sarkar said several teachers had left after failing to secure MPO benefits for the college section.
"The college section is not doing well. There is a shortage of both teachers and students. It would be better if it were closed," he said.
Governing body Chairman Parimal Kirtan said he had received his appointment letter only a week earlier and had yet to visit the institution or hold a meeting.
"I do not know much about these issues," he said.
Upazila Secondary Education Officer Mahfuza Begum said her office was responsible for supervising secondary-level education, not the college section. She said the Dhaka regional office was responsible for overseeing the college section.
Muksudpur Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO) Mahmud Ashik Kabir said he was aware that only one student had appeared in the HSC examination from the institution and failed.
"We will investigate the matter," he said.

item.title: UIU collaborates on Robo Fest 2026 in Jamalpur
item.description:
A day-long robotics festival, Robo Fest 2026, was held in Jamalpur on Sunday to introduce students to robotics, artificial intelligence and emerging technologies through interactive exhibitions and hands-on learning.
Organized by the Science and Innovation Club of United Public School & College, Jamalpur, and United Trust, in collaboration with United International University (UIU), the festival was held under the theme “A Journey into the World of Robotics”.
The festival featured technological innovations and projects developed by UIU’s Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Robotics (CAIR), including the UIU Mars Rover, UIU Aerial Robotics, UIU Rescue Rover and UIU Mariner.
Students from United Public School & College, M A Rashid Memorial Academy and M A Gafur Memorial Academy in Jamalpur participated in the event.
CAIR members presented innovations across 3 major areas of robotics: ground, marine and aerial. The ground robotics segment featured the Mars Rover and Rescue Rover, while the marine segment showcased the UIU Mariner. The UIU Aerial Robotics team also demonstrated its technologies and activities.
Students and visitors had the opportunity to learn about the mechanisms and practical applications of the showcased projects.
The exhibition also highlighted UIU teams' achievements in international competitions. The UIU Mars Rover team secured third place globally and first place in Asia at the University Rover Challenge (URC) 2026, along with the “Best Autonomous System Recognition” award.
The achievement marked a milestone for Bangladesh and was recognized as a unique accomplishment in the 20-year history of rover competitions in Asia.
Meanwhile, the UIU Aerial Robotics team secured fourth place globally at the Student Unmanned Aerial Systems (SUAS) 2026 competition, becoming the first Bangladeshi team to participate in the event.
The festival aimed to develop students' innovative thinking, creativity and problem-solving skills while encouraging their interest in science and technology. It also provided opportunities to gain practical knowledge of robotics, programming, artificial intelligence and engineering design.
Through initiatives such as Robo Fest 2026, the organizers seek to encourage students in Jamalpur to explore emerging technologies and participate in national and international science, programming and robotics competitions.

Best time to eat chia seeds
item.description:
Many of us kick-start our day with chia seeds. In contact with water, they take on a jelly-like form, which helps increase the feeling of fullness in the stomach and keeps you feeling full for longer. However, you can get their nutritional benefits not only in the morning but at any time of the day.
You can eat chia seeds mixed with yogurt, smoothies, oats, fruit, or pudding. They can also be added to soups, salads, and pancakes. However, there is one thing you must keep in mind before eating them: do not eat dry chia seeds directly. They absorb water quickly and swell up, which carries a risk of getting stuck in the throat. So it is safest to eat them soaked in water or another liquid, or mixed with a moist food such as yogurt.

item.title: The secret to spotless, fresh-smelling kitchen towels
item.description:
While cooking, curry spills or oil and turmeric splatter inside the microwave. Kitchen towels are often the first thing people reach for to clean up such messes. However, regular use can cause grease and dirt to build up in the fabric, leaving stubborn stains and unpleasant odours.
If not cleaned properly, damp and dirty towels can also create an environment where germs thrive.
To deal with this problem, many people repeatedly boil their towels in hot water or use different cleaning products. However, excessive heat or improper washing methods can damage the fabric's colour and texture. Keeping kitchen towels clean therefore requires proper care.
Here are some simple ways to remove grease stains and unpleasant odours using common household ingredients.
When oil, gravy or other food spills onto a kitchen towel, it is best to clean it as soon as possible. Once a stain dries, it can become trapped in the fabric fibres, making it more difficult to remove.
First, gently blot away excess oil or food particles with a tissue. Then rinse the stained area with water. To remove grease stains, apply a small amount of dishwashing liquid and leave it for 10 to 15 minutes. Gently scrub the area before rinsing it thoroughly.
For turmeric or tomato stains, make a paste by mixing a little baking soda with water. Apply the paste to the stain, leave it for a while and then rinse. However, it is advisable to test the mixture on a small, hidden area first, especially when dealing with coloured or delicate fabrics.
Soaking kitchen towels before washing can help loosen dirt, especially if they have been used for a long time or have accumulated excessive grease. Take a container of warm water suitable for the fabric and mix in detergent according to the product instructions. Soak the towels for some time, adjusting the duration according to the fabric type and level of dirt.
Baking soda can also help reduce unpleasant odours and assist with cleaning in certain cases. For removing stains from white fabrics, check the product instructions and fabric care guidelines before using hydrogen peroxide. It may cause coloured fabrics to fade. Always follow safety instructions before combining any cleaning products.
Kitchen towels usually come into contact with grease, food residue and different types of dirt. Therefore, it is better to wash them separately from everyday clothing.
Use water at the temperature recommended on the fabric care label, along with a suitable detergent. Although cotton towels can generally withstand relatively high temperatures, not all fabrics are suitable for washing in boiling water.
After washing, make sure no soap or detergent residue remains on the towels. This helps keep the fabric clean and prevents discomfort during use.
If kitchen towels still smell unpleasant after washing, they may need more thorough cleaning and proper drying. In some cases, white vinegar can help reduce unwanted odours. However, it is not a substitute for detergent. Before using it, check whether it is suitable for the fabric and follow the product instructions.
Caution: Never mix vinegar with bleach or other cleaning products, as this can trigger harmful chemical reactions.
Completely drying kitchen towels after washing is essential. Whenever possible, hang them outdoors or in direct sunlight. Leaving damp towels folded or in a moist environment for extended periods can cause unpleasant odours to develop.
After each use, hang towels in a place with good air circulation. Avoid using the same towel for too long and replace it regularly as needed.
Developing simple habits such as changing kitchen towels regularly, washing them separately from other clothes, and ensuring they are completely dry can make it easier to maintain cleanliness. These practices help reduce grease stains and unpleasant odours while keeping the kitchen more hygienic.

Performance of a lifetime
item.description:
Theatre is often reduced to performance. An actor memorizes lines, puts on a costume, and inhabits a life long enough to make it convincing. We tend to assume that is what makes it theatrical: the act of becoming someone else. But performance is only one part of it.
A theatre also has a director, a script, critics, rehearsals, and an audience. It is, in essence, an institution built around visibility. Nothing in it means much until someone is there to witness it.
Femininity works the same way.
Not merely as performance, but as an existence continually arranged around spectatorship.
I felt it countless times. I felt that before I had words for it.
I was in a theatre with my family, waiting for the lights to go down, knees apart, when my mother leaned over.
“Girls don’t sit like that,” she said, gently.
She wasn’t angry. The correction came wrapped in concern. I knew what she meant: close my knees and take up less space. So, I did.
The play hadn’t even started, and I had already been reviewed.
We talk about femininity as something a woman simply has, a natural pull towards softness and grace, as if it grew out of the body unprompted. But nobody walks onto a stage already knowing the script. A girl learns hers through correction.
Sometimes from her close ones, sometimes from strangers. She learns which emotions make her too much and which make her agreeable. Her anger is unbecoming, but her empathy must be limitless.
She is told that her confidence is only admirable to a certain extent; that must stop once it begins to resemble authority. She is taught that beauty is rewarded not because it reveals character, but because it reassures an audience.
Over time they pile up, and one day the rehearsal stops feeling like a rehearsal. It feels like instinct.
That is ideology’s best trick: repetition passes for nature.
But performance alone cannot sustain theater. It requires an audience.
It needs someone to watch the fall.
The audience never needs to say a word. The actress fixes her posture because she knows she’s being watched. She hears the applause before it comes and the criticism before it’s spoken.
Girls learn this in the doorway, before they’ve entered any room.
Is my orna in the right place? Is my hair okay? Is this too much blush?
Checking what their bodies might be saying about them.
Under a watchful gaze, femininity does not bloom--it shrivels. The gaze arrives long before the observer. And at one stage, it no longer matters whether anyone has stayed to watch--the eyes, they’ve turned inwards.
Feminism named this long before it had language sophisticated enough to describe it: surveillance, prolonged enough, becomes self-surveillance.
The critic never leaves the theatre; he leaves his gaze in his old seat. And that is enough.
Maybe that’s why debates about femininity so often collapse into the question of choice, mistaking the structure for the performance. The interesting question is not whether the actress enjoys her costume, but whether she chose the stage at all.
Agency and structure are not opposites. A woman can be soft, kind, and forgiving. She can love dresses and flowers and lipstick, and none of it makes her smaller.
Those pleasures are real, even if they live inside a culture that rewards them.
Expectation doesn’t cancel out desire, and desire doesn’t make expectation disappear.
Both can be true at once. The two can coexist.
That is where femininity is most often misunderstood. Feminism isn’t suspicious of it because it is artificial.
Everything human is constructed to some extent:Language, law, nations. That doesn’t make any of it less significant.
What feminism questions is not the performance but the conditions under which it becomes compulsory. A role stops being expressive the moment leaving it is punished.
Perhaps that is what separates theatre from captivity.
In a theatre, the curtain always falls.
The actor takes off the costume, the audience goes home, and the role stays behind on the stage where it belongs.
Femininity has never given women that. It follows them off the stage and into mirrors, classrooms, relationships, every photograph ever taken, every family dinner ever sat through.
The stage follows them home, then one day it becomes home.
That’s why it can be exhausting even when you love it, even when you chose it. Not because it’s fake, but because there is no intermission.
I have a niece who is one. She can’t walk yet, and she has no opinion about colours. I wanted to buy her a doll, and I was scrolling through gifts marked “for
girls” before I even noticed. Then I stopped.
When did I start looking in this aisle? Why not a ball? A toy car? Why was I already steering her world towards pink?
Maybe feminism’s most radical move was never to tear down the theatre. Maybe it was to imagine a world where the actress can walk off the stage and still be recognized as herself.
Until then, the script keeps travelling, not through villains but through the people who love us. And through us.
Shuchi Binte Shahjalal is a writer who writes gently, honestly, and just a little dangerously about love and home.

item.title: The brown woman’s dilemma
item.description:
Award acceptance speeches often open with the recipient’s gratitude for one person: their mother. It is fitting. Mothers are where everything we know begins. They are the life-givers, the most tangible evidence we have of a creator. And for many of us, mothers shape our lives from beginning to end.
My mother’s stories were etched into every hall I grew up in.
From New York to Lusaka to Dhaka to Hanoi to Seoul to Port Moresby, and in the many homes and hotel rooms between, there were countless halls. Where my mother’s boundless insight fell short, I hounded the doors of the only other sages I knew: my aunts, my grandmothers, my sisters, and at times even my female teachers.
The more I sought, the more their insight felt like a confirmation of my responsibility to live for them.
Only now, older, do I see how little these women were allowed to live.
Lately, I am fascinated by bounds: boundaries, binding, and the shapes we form when we bind.
I have filled tens of books and notebooks between 2010 and 2026, most of them spiral-bound. The spiral weaves from hole to hole and tightens, tracing a circle that repeats the same shape but, funnily enough, never ends up quite where it began.
Around 2013, in a Dubai shopping mall, my father spotted a bright pink book with etchings of a mermaid, flowers, and butterflies adorning the cover.It was called Girls’ Miscellany: Fascinating Information Every Girl Should Know.He asked me if I wanted it.
“Oh, no, Baba,”
I shook my head, because that was how my mother usually responded to generous offers. It’s a habit I still have today.
To be a woman and directly ask for what you want remains unsettling to me. Really, I wanted that book. I liked books, mermaids, flowers, butterflies, and hot pink. I was intrigued by the large, unfamiliar word in the title.
At my denial, my father shook his head at the cashier.
“She doesn’t want it.”
What?
He wasn’t playing the game right.
“Wait. I changed my mind!”
I carried that book around with me for so long that its spine came loose. Pages grew thin and stained. I had memorized everything “miscellaneous” about its contents, including the long and dismal list of Henry Tudor’s wives--victims of his frustration at his own failure to bear a son.
And the fact that for centuries, women in ancient Chinese tradition were coerced into binding their feet and violently constricting the natural growth of their bones to gain a daintier appearance. It was called foot binding. “Pretty”, as a replacement for autonomy. “Woman”, as a replacement for “human”.
Boundaries are something I learned about in therapy. I was first brought to therapy when I was too young to understand what it was. In New York City, my mother would enter a large hall with mahogany wall-to-ceiling doors that slowly swung shut.
The doors swallowed her for about an hour while I played computer games with a friendly man outside.
I thought I was accompanying my mom while she spoke to lawyers about the mean things my Baba was doing.
Really, she was consulting lawyers regarding his pitiful crimes, both legal and moral, while her daughter spoke to a child therapist.
Eleven years later, therapists told me that boundaries were what healthy people used to avoid carrying the pain their mothers had endured at the hands of fathers, sons, misogynistic bosses, and so on.
Part of me distrusted this idea.
Before anything else, I am my mother’s daughter. What kind of living comes at the cost of betrayal?
A boundary seemed akin to shutting the doors to the years of love, sacrifice, good humor, and good grief that bound me to my mother.
Bangladeshi women know well that womanhood often strings up and binds women in hereditary ways.
I feel the pressures and pains my aunt, sisters, and mother have had to live through because, unfortunately, patriarchy is crafted of things far tougher than plastic.
This inherited baggage lives off the idea that self- sacrifice is a virtue.
The pains I inherited from living through women who don’t live caused me to idolize martyrdom.
As someone so connected to bounds, boundaries are still new to me. Boundaries don’t feel like they were made for someone like me, someone who is a woman and is Brown.But the older I get, the more I’m having to accept being self-defining in my identity. More and more, angering others feels like the price I have to pay for living.
Selfishness is a “crime”, and yet the self is all I have.
Is the selfish Brown Woman, then, nothing at all?
Deya Nurani is a freelance contributor based in the US.

Police detain several over unrest in Savar, Ashulia
item.description:
Police have detained several people from different areas of Savar and Ashulia over allegations of vandalism, attacks on garment factories and attempts to create unrest amid ongoing workers’ protests, Dhaka District Police Superintendent Shamima Pervin said on Monday.
However, she could not immediately confirm the number of people detained, saying arrests had been made separately by industrial police and police from Ashulia and Savar police stations.
Speaking to journalists in front of a factory in Jamgora on the Ashulia-Baipail road in the afternoon, Shamima said those accused of trying to vandalise vehicles, attack garment factories, injure workers and hurl brickbats had been detained.
She said police teams were still conducting operations and that the total number of arrests would be confirmed after information from different units was compiled in the evening.
Dhaka Range Deputy Inspector General (DIG) Md Mostafizur Rahman, who was also present during the visit, said the police would take strict legal action against those creating instability in the industrial belt and those backing them.
He said the government had formed a wage board for garment workers on Sunday and that it had already started its work to address wage-related concerns through the legal process.
“Those who are creating instability despite the formation of the wage board are not, in our view, part of the workers’ movement. They are people creating disorder in society, and strict legal action will be taken against them,” he said.
The DIG urged workers to return to their jobs without fear and called on factory owners to resume normal operations, assuring them that police would ensure security at factories.
He said police were collecting information about those allegedly instigating the unrest from behind the scenes, adding that no one would be allowed to act outside the law. Those involved in vandalism and arson at factories and other locations were being identified, and cases and arrests were underway, he added.
Addressing rumours that a worker had been killed by police gunfire, Mostafizur said no such incident had occurred and accused a group of spreading misinformation on social media to destabilise the country and mislead workers.
He urged journalists to report verified information, saying false claims could create confusion among workers and the public. He also warned that legal action would be taken against anyone spreading misleading information or inciting unrest, including labour leaders or others providing financial support.
The DIG said police had been monitoring several social media groups for the past four days, alleging that they were circulating provocative messages announcing demonstrations at specific locations for the following day.
He also expressed concern over the safety of students during the unrest, saying a student was injured by bricks thrown by protesters while trying to flee near a school at the Bangladesh Krira Shikkha Protishthan (BKSP) on Monday.
Mostafizur said a large number of police personnel had been deployed across the industrial belt, including uniformed and plainclothes officers, members of the Armed Police Battalion (APBn) and the RRF.
He said workers in some factories had initially entered their workplaces before gradually stopping work. After general leave was declared at the factories, they took to the streets to protest.

item.title: Home minister holds meeting with garment owners to resolve workers' unrest
item.description:
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed on Monday held a meeting at the Secretariat with leaders of garment factory owners as part of the government's efforts to resolve the ongoing unrest in the readymade garment (RMG) sector and restore normalcy in industrial areas.
The meeting was convened following Sunday's violent demonstrations by garment workers in Dhaka, Gazipur, Savar, Ashulia and Tangail, where protesters demanded a minimum monthly wage of Tk30,000.
The government has taken initiatives to address the situation through dialogue with industry stakeholders while maintaining law and order and ensuring the uninterrupted operation of the country's vital export-oriented garment sector.
During Sunday's demonstrations, several areas witnessed clashes between protesters and law enforcement personnel, road blockades and incidents of vandalism targeting factories and vehicles.
Meanwhile, police arrested 19 leaders and activists of the Awami League and its affiliated organisations, including the banned Bangladesh Chhatra League and Jubo League, in Dhaka on allegations of instigating the demonstrations.
The government has also formed a six-member minimum wage board to review the existing salary structure of garment workers, with representation from workers, employers, the government and an independent member.
At present, the minimum monthly wage for garment workers stands at Tk12,500. Workers are demanding Tk30,000, citing rising living costs, including house rent, food, transportation and healthcare expenses.
The government has called upon workers to return to their workplaces and pursue their demands through dialogue and peaceful negotiations, rather than resorting to violence, vandalism and road blockades.
The BGMEA has expressed concern that prolonged unrest could disrupt production, delay export shipments and affect Bangladesh's commitments to international buyers.

item.title: Police disperse garment workers after fresh clashes in Mirpur
item.description:
Clashes broke out between garment workers and police again in the capital’s Mirpur area on Monday morning, as police moved to disperse workers attempting to gather on the roads.
At around 9:15am, police chased away workers who had taken positions on the road. As of the latest reports, confrontations between the two sides were continuing.
Hafizur Rahman, officer-in-charge of Mirpur police station, confirmed the incident, saying: “The workers came to block the road, and we dispersed them.”
Earlier on Sunday, garment workers clashed with police during protests demanding a minimum monthly wage of Tk30,000.
On Monday morning, when workers attempted to gather again in the Mirpur-10 area, police intervened, triggering a series of chases and counter-chases. Workers threw bricks and stones at police, who responded by firing tear gas shells.
The workers were subsequently dispersed, but tension remained high across the area. Most shops remained closed, while police restricted people from gathering on the streets and questioned individuals they considered suspicious.

item.title: Garment workers block Dhaka-Tangail highway again, traffic halted
item.description:
Garment workers blocked the Dhaka-Tangail highway in Gazipur again on Monday, demanding a minimum monthly wage of Tk30,000 and bringing traffic to a standstill.
The blockade began around 8:30am, when workers from several factories gathered on the highway in the Palli Bidyut area.
Mohammad Amjad Hossain, superintendent of Gazipur Industrial Police, said around 1,000 workers occupied the highway at the time, halting traffic in both directions.
He said Industrial Police and other law enforcement agencies were working to bring the situation under control and restore traffic movement.
On Sunday, workers staged protests in Konabari, Safipur, Palli Bidyut and surrounding industrial areas, demanding the same wage increase.
Workers and police clashed intermittently, escalating tensions at several locations. Protesters also set fire to a police box and vandalized several vehicles.
The unrest disrupted traffic on the Dhaka-Tangail highway for around six hours on Sunday.

item.title: 10 BGB platoons deployed in Gazipur, 21 magistrates assigned
item.description:
Ten platoons of Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) have been deployed in Gazipur to maintain law and order amid ongoing garment workers’ protests demanding a minimum monthly wage of Tk30,000. They are being assisted by 21 executive magistrates.
Arif Hossain, assistant commissioner of the Media and Research Cell at the Gazipur deputy commissioner’s office, confirmed the deployment in a message sent to the “Media Cell DC of Gazipur” group at 8:26am on Monday.
Sources at the deputy commissioner’s office and Industrial Police said Industrial Police, district police, BGB personnel and executive magistrates were working together to keep the situation under control.
Amjad Hossain, superintendent of Gazipur Industrial Police, said around 1,500 workers gathered in the Palli Bidyut area along the Dhaka-Tangail highway at around 8:30am on Monday, bringing traffic to a standstill.
BGB personnel, Industrial Police and other law enforcement agencies have been deployed in Chandra, Palli Bidyut, Safipur, Konabari and Mouchak to manage the situation and restore traffic movement, he added.
Garment workers in Gazipur have been protesting for the past two days, demanding a minimum monthly wage of Tk30,000. Thousands of workers have occupied the highway at different points, halting traffic and causing severe inconvenience to long-distance bus passengers and other commuters.
The protests initially involved road blockades in Mouchak, Safipur and the Chandra-Palli Bidyut areas of Kaliakair, bringing traffic on the Dhaka-Tangail highway to a complete halt.
During the unrest, gates of several factories in the Palli Bidyut area of Kaliakair were vandalized. A police box was also vandalized in Mouchak, another was set on fire beneath the Konabari flyover, and a pickup van was torched in front of the Ansar Academy.
The unrest later spread to nearby industrial areas, including Ratanpur, Konabari and Kashimpur. Operations at around 30 factories in these areas were suspended amid the protests.

item.title: Clashes break out between garment workers, police in Ashulia
item.description:
Clashes broke out between garment workers and police in Ashulia, Savar, on Monday, prompting police to fire several rounds of tear gas shells to disperse the protesters.
No casualties were immediately reported. Following the clashes, workers and police remained in a standoff.
The incident occurred after 10am in the Narsinghapur and Nishchintapur areas along the Abdullahpur-Baipail road. Most factories along the road declared a general holiday amid the unrest.
According to witnesses, workers initially gathered in front of a factory owned by Ananta Group before moving to a Hamim Group factory, where they allegedly threw bricks.
Tensions escalated when the workers attempted to block the road to press home their demands, triggering a confrontation with law enforcement personnel and subsequent clashes.
Police fired several rounds of tear gas shells in an effort to disperse the workers and bring the situation under control.
Shoeb Ahmed, additional superintendent of police (operations and intelligence) at Industrial Police-1, said police were working to restore order.
A tense situation prevailed in the area at the time of filing this report, with additional police personnel deployed to maintain law and order.

item.title: Gold prices rise by Tk3,194 per bhori after two days
item.description:
The Bangladesh Jewellers Association (Bajus) has raised gold prices in the domestic market, just two days after announcing a reduction, citing an increase in the price of pure gold in the local market.
The new rates came into effect at 10am on Monday. Under the revised prices, 22-carat hallmarked gold costs Tk18,935 per gram, or Tk220,786 per bhori (11.664 grams), including VAT.
The decision was taken at a meeting of the Bajus Standing Committee on Pricing and Price Monitoring on Monday morning, chaired by its chairman, Dr Dewan Aminul Islam Shahin.
According to the new price list, 21-carat gold costs Tk18,085 per gram, or Tk210,871 per bhori. The price of 18-carat gold has been set at Tk15,535 per gram, or Tk181,128 per bhori.
Gold made using traditional methods now costs Tk12,690 per gram, or Tk147,932 per bhori.
On Saturday, Bajus reduced the price of 22-carat gold by Tk5,481 per bhori, bringing it to Tk217,592, including VAT. The revised rate also took effect at 10am that day.
With Monday’s increase, the price of 22-carat gold has risen by Tk3,194 per bhori from the previous rate.
Bajus has also announced new prices for silver ornaments. The price of 22-carat silver has been set at Tk300 per gram, including VAT. The rates for 21-carat and 18-carat silver are Tk290 and Tk250 per gram, respectively, while silver made using traditional methods costs Tk190 per gram.
Bajus said making charges would depend on the design and craftsmanship of the jewellery. As VAT is included in the fixed retail prices, it cannot be charged separately.
For exchanges of old gold jewellery, 12% of the value must be deducted, excluding making charges and the cost of stones. For the purchase of old jewellery, the deduction will be 18%. VAT cannot be deducted separately in either transaction.
The revised prices will remain in effect at jewellery shops across the country until further notice.

Petrobangla: Fire at Inani gas well may take 15 days to control
item.description:
It may take up to 15 days for the fire triggered by a gas blowout at a deep well in Chhota Inani of Cox's Bazar to subside, Petrobangla has said.
The fire broke out on October 27 when gas erupted from underground during drilling operations at a depth of around 1,000 feet near Chhota Inani Bridge in Jaliapalong Union of Ukhiya Upazila.
According to a Petrobangla press release issued on Sunday, two geologists from the Bangladesh Petroleum Exploration and Production Company Limited (BAPEX) have been sent to monitor the situation. They are currently stationed in Cox's Bazar to oversee developments.
On the advice of experts, the gas is being allowed to escape freely to prevent the fire from spreading. The intensity of the blaze is expected to gradually decline over the next 15 days.
If the gas flow does not decrease within this period, the expert team will take alternative measures, including firefighting operations and steps to stop the flow, the release said.
As a precautionary measure, public access within a 100-metre radius of the well has been prohibited. Local authorities have also taken necessary steps to maintain law and order.
Petrobangla, BAPEX and the local administration are jointly monitoring the situation round the clock.
Meanwhile, geological and 2D seismic surveys are underway to assess the potential gas reserves in the surrounding area.
Petrobangla has urged people not to panic, remain cautious and cooperate with the authorities.

item.title: Filipino woman injured in Banani gas leak fire dies
item.description:
A 32-year-old Filipino woman who suffered severe burns in a fire caused by a gas leak in the capital’s Banani area has died while undergoing treatment.
Keistin Ver Bunag died at around 3:30am on Tuesday at the National Institute of Burn and Plastic Surgery.
She had suffered burns to 63% of her body, while her respiratory tract was also damaged by smoke or hot gases.
Dr Sultan Mahmud Shikdar, a resident surgeon (emergency) at the institute, said Keistin was admitted to its emergency department on October 28 after being referred from Continental Hospital.
According to preliminary information, she sustained the injuries at around 7am that day while attempting to light a gas stove.
Her condition remained critical following admission. Despite receiving treatment and close medical attention, she could not be saved, the doctor said.

item.title: Antonelli becomes youngest Formula One world champion
item.description:
Kimi Antonelli drove the perfect race to finish third in his Mercedes at the Mexico Grand Prix and seal his place in Formula One history as the youngest world champion.
Max Verstappen took the chequered flag but all eyes were on the young Italian who takes the crown at the age of 20 years and 68 days, more than three years younger than Sebastian Vettel in 2010.
He is the first Italian to win the title since Alberto Ascari in 1953.
"We did it. I wouldn't be here without Mercedes, without my family," said an emotional Antonelli who has won nine races so far this season.
"I am very grateful for this moment, it will be with me forever. I am speechless, just trying to process what happened.
"It's been an incredible season and to share this podium with Max and Lewis (Hamilton) is incredible. I am looking forward to some more battles in the future."
The race broke into two parts as it was suspended after 46 of the 71 laps following a crash involving Cadillac's Valtteri Bottas.
The Finn's suspension on the front left side had collapsed causing his wheel to buckle and making him a helpless passenger as his car flew backwards off the track and slammed into the barriers.
The 37-year-old Bottas was slow to emerge from his car but waved to the crowd as he walked away, with all the other cars returning to the pits to await a restart.
Antonelli, who needed just to finish in the top nine to seal the title, was running third in his Mercedes when the race was stopped behind Red Bull's Verstappen and the Ferrari of Charles Leclerc.
His nearest challenger teammate George Russell was out of the running after suffering a poor start dropping from second on the grid to fifth and struggling with his power.
Russell had to win to have any hope of prolonging the title race.
Lewis Hamilton, who started on pole and also needed to win to push Antonelli, was furious with his Ferrari teammate after an incident at the start that saw Leclerc leave the track and steal the lead. The Monegasque was handed a five-second penalty but he retained track superiority over Hamilton.
That changed on the restart when Hamilton powered past Antonelli and Leclerc and bumped wheels with Verstappen before settling into second.
There was a further yellow flag when the Racing Bull of Arvid Lindblad also crashed out 10 laps from the end after tangling with the McLaren of Oscar Piastri.
Antonelli sat tight in third as Hamilton continued to press Verstappen. It was entirely appropriate that the young Italian, in tears as he crossed the line, was led in by two of the all-time great drivers with 11 championships between them.

item.title: Mbappe strikes after China controversy as Real beat Santander
item.description:
Kylian Mbappe moved on from a tumultuous week by scoring a penalty to help Real Madrid win 3-0 at Racing Santander on Sunday.
The French forward narrowly lost out on the Ballon d'Or to Bayern Munich's Harry Kane on Monday and then had to apologise after a social media storm following a video in which he joked about former Chinese leader Mao Zedong.
Real Madrid's match, along with other Spanish fixtures this weekend, was not broadcast by Chinese state television because of the fallout.
Jude Bellingham and Yan Diomande were also on target to keep third-place Madrid within three points of leaders Barcelona, who thrashed Alaves 6-1 on Saturday.
Jose Mourinho's side have won six straight games across all competitions and are a point behind city rivals Atletico Madrid, who beat Levante 2-0.
"In the first half we were very strong, we came out to play well," Mourinho told reporters.
"The team is growing, playing well, I think we should have scored even more goals with the chances we had."
Mbappe won a soft penalty as he went down under little pressure from Matteo Prati, smashing it home to put Madrid ahead at the Sardinero stadium in the 11th minute.
It was the 27-year-old's 12th league goal of the season, trailing only Barcelona's Raphinha with 15 in the scoring charts.
Madrid had control of the game and a fine pass from Arda Guler sent Bellingham through on goal for the second.
The England international knocked the ball past the goalkeeper and rolled home for his 50th goal since joining Madrid in 2023.
"Reaching 50 goals with Real Madrid is very special," Bellingham told Real Madrid TV.
"We played very well. It was very important to win after the victory at Camp Nou (against Barca last weekend), so we are very happy."
Guler spurned a good opportunity for the third after being set up by Mbappe, before Madrid's record signing Diomande lashed home from the edge of the box.
The hosts started the second half well, pushing Madrid back, much to the chagrin of Mourinho, who yelled at his players.
Madrid regained their control and racked up several more chances, with Mbappe hitting the post and Bellingham denied by Racing goalkeeper Julen Agirrezabala.
Racing won a penalty after Madrid's Aurelien Tchouameni handled in the box, but the award was cancelled after a VAR review.
Bellingham had a second goal ruled out in stoppage time after he strayed offside before finding the net and Endrick bent an effort narrowly wide from distance.
Hosts Racing, 16th, back in La Liga for the first time in 14 seasons, fell to their first home defeat of the campaign.
Earlier Sevilla, sixth, suffered a 3-1 loss at Getafe, who moved into mid-table.
"(Madrid's penalty award) annoys me," Racing coach Jose Alberto told DAZN.
"Evidently we came across a great Madrid, who put us under a lot of pressure in the first half hour, and were much better than us, but what conditions everything was the first goal and the penalty."
Valencia, 19th, beat Elche 1-0 with a well-taken goal from Umar Sadiq to move to within a point of safety after a bad start to the season.
Elsewhere Athletic Bilbao, seventh, edged fifth-place Real Sociedad 2-1 in an entertaining Basque derby clash at San Mames stadium.
Inaki Williams lobbed Athletic ahead early on before Luka Sucic drilled home from the edge of the box to level.
Alex Berenguer controversially restored Athletic's advantage just before half-time from the penalty spot, after Jon Aramburu was adjudged to have fouled Nico Williams, although he appeared to win the ball.
"I think it's incredible that a penalty like that is given when I touched the ball, even Nico said it," complained Aramburu to DAZN.
Spanish World Cup-winning goalkeeper Unai Simon made several fine saves to ensure Los Leones claimed the three points.
